No source in this session confirms a lake or pollution example in the book, so it is omitted from facts and from the story. What is supported by several summaries and reader highlights is the bathtub model: stock (water in the tub), inflow (faucet), outflow (drain); a stock changes slowly even when flows change suddenly; stocks act as delays, buffers or shock absorbers; a stock can be raised by closing the outflow as well as opening the inflow. The remark that the faucet takes a second to turn but the tub takes minutes to fill comes from a summary, not verified in the book text. The soil-over-centuries image is from a reader highlight and is left out of facts. No numbers are used. The lake appears only as an invented everyday example in the lesson, not as a book fact.
facts: Meadows starts with the simplest system she can draw: a bathtub. The water in the tub is the stock, the faucet is the inflow, the drain is the outflow.
Turning the faucet takes a second, but filling the tub takes minutes: the hand moves fast and the water level follows slowly.
The level changes only through the difference between what flows in and what flows out; if both are equal, the level stays where it is.
A stock can be raised by closing the drain as well as by opening the faucet: there is more than one way to fill a bathtub.
Stocks change slowly even when the flows into or out of them change suddenly.
Because of that, stocks act as delays, buffers or shock absorbers: they let inflow and outflow be out of balance with each other for a while.
Meadows notes that these time lags can cause trouble in a system, but they can also be a source of stability.
Stocks are the elements of a system that you can see, feel, count or measure at a given moment; in the tub, the water level.
In a feedback loop, a delay makes the system likely to swing back and forth, because the information it acts on arrives late.
scene_details: a bathtub with the faucet open and the drain open
the hand turns the tap in a second, the water takes minutes to rise
the water level as the thing you can see and measure
tension: You can change the flow in a second, but the thing you actually care about, the level, answers much later.
opening_idea: Open on the bathtub: a hand turns the faucet in a second while the water level takes minutes to move.

lessons.idea: Judge a change by what it does to the stock, not by whether the level has moved yet; a level lags behind the flow.
lessons.anchor: the faucet turned in a second and the tub filling over minutes

reflect_final: Which change you made recently might you be judging too early, because the level you are watching has not had time to respond to the new flow?

use_cases.situation: A new process started last week and a colleague wants to scrap it.
use_cases.move: Say the flow changed on day one but the level takes longer to show, and agree on when you will look at the level.

use_cases.situation: You started spending less on takeaway and the account looks the same.
use_cases.move: Check the balance only at the next statement and compare it with the one before.

use_cases.situation: A family member started sleeping earlier and is still tired.
use_cases.move: Say the tub fills slower than the tap turns, and ask how they feel in a few days.

pocket_idea: A faucet turns in a second and a tub fills in minutes: judge a new habit by the level, and give the level time.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: You can open a faucet in a second, but the water in the tub rises on its own schedule.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Meadows begins with a bathtub: the water is the stock, the faucet the inflow, the drain the outflow. You can turn the tap in a second, but the level follows slowly, and it only moves by the gap between in and out. So stocks behave like buffers, which is why a good change can look like nothing for a while.
